Posted May 31, 2002
(MarijuanaNews note: My friend Dan Forbes is the preeminent investigative journalist in the uncovering of DEAland Drug War scandals.

Sadly, he doesn't have much competition in that field. Thirty years ago, Woodward and Bernstein's investigation at the Washington Post of the Watergate burglary inspired a whole generation of journalism students, who thought that they could make a difference. Alas, that was not to be, and certainly not at the Washington Post.

Instead, the drug war has suppressed any questioning of governmental subversion of the democratic process and the fundamental liberties of the American people.

Sometime I become frustrated when even anti-prohibitionists cannot see that the Drug War has become an end in itself with huge vested interests in continuing war without end.

Dan Forbes has documented another aspect of this process. This is a very important story. It will be interesting to see if any of our watchdogs in the established media pick it up. I go to the Washington Post's web site every day, so my time won't be entirely wasted when I look for something about it there. One of the greatest ironies of the last thirty years is that the paper that brought down Richard Nixon has played such a crucial role in maintaining his most disastrous and dishonest domestic program, making cannabis prohibition the heart of the Drug War.

Congratulations to Dan Forbes on a job very well done.

And to Governor Taft of Ohio, shame on you for betraying the principles of limited government with which his family has been identified for a century.)

PRESS RELEASE
MAY 30, 2002
Media Contact: Daniel Forbes:

Ohio Governor Bob Taft and the highest reaches of his administration have embarked on a concerted, months-long effort to subvert the state's electoral process. With overall control of budgets, jobs and sentencing policy at stake, the Taft administration has organized a sophisticated, sub-rosa campaign to defeat a drug treatment rather than incarceration amendment likely to appear on the ballot in November.

A four-month long Institute for Policy Studies investigation by freelance journalist Daniel Forbes details political malfeasance, the misuse of public funds and the inappropriate use of government resources in Ohio. The effort has been aided by federal officials, including President Bush's publicly announced nominee to be deputy director of the White House drug czar's office (since confirmed), and a senior U.S. Senate staffer. The drug czars of Florida and Michigan and a senior Drug Enforcement Administration agent also participated in the scheme.

Ohio officials consulted with and enlisted the aid of the wife of the former finance chair of the Republican National Committee, who herself has played a key political role for Jeb Bush, as well as several taxpayer-supported, staunch anti-drug organizations, including the supposedly apolitical Partnership for a Drug-Free America. The Partnership was slated to produce TV ads to sway public opinion in favor of the Ohio drug-policy status quo. Its four top executives advised the Taft administration during a day-long strategy session hosted by that Senate staffer and held in the U.S. Capitol building itself.

The effort has entailed hundreds of staff-hours of state-paid time. Last fall, Ohio's first lady, cabinet officials and senior staffers in the governor's office attended weekly strategy sessions on the public's dime. State funds paid for out of town trips and overnight lodging, and the administration even proposed to divert U.S. Department of Justice crime-fighting grants to fund their nascent campaign's eventual polling, focus groups and advertising. A mid-October strategy session held at the governor's residence in Columbus was attended by 19 senior officials and private executives from Ohio, Michigan and Florida. (A similar referendum will likely be on the ballot in Michigan; in Florida, proponents have postponed their effort.)

Modeled on a similar measure, Proposition 36, that passed overwhelmingly in California in 2000, the Ohio referendum proposes to offer treatment rather than prison to defendants charged with a first or second instance of simple drug possession. It's backed by the same rich trio - billionaires, George Soros and Peter Lewis, and multimillionaire John Sperling - who have successfully financed drug reform initiatives since 1996, including Prop. 36, and several medical marijuana measures. Should the Taft effort succeed, it will work to maintain the Ohio status quo of incarcerating a disproportionate number of racial minorities for possessing small, personal use amounts of drugs.

The revelations from Ohio question the probity of the Partnership for a Drug-Free America, which partners with the White House in a controversial, nearly $2-billion (total-value) anti-drug advertising and media content campaign. The media campaign has recently come under attack from Drug Czar John P. Walters himself as being ineffectual. Its second, five-year appropriation currently under congressional review, will Congress now take another look at a program whose private strategic partner, the PDFA, was willing to insert itself improperly into an election in Ohio?
